item.title: You Want It Darker
item.description:
Leonard Cohen died in November of 2016, a mere few weeks after the release of his last record, You Want it Darker. The homonymous song of that record greatly surprised me, and revealed to me a Leonard Cohen that I was previously unaware of.

When I like the art produced by an artist, I tend to confine my interest to the art, rather than the artist. I guess I learned this lesson as a teenager, in the early nineteen-eighties, from the first book I ever bought, using my own pocket money: No One Here Gets Out Alive, the life and death of Jim Morrison. Contrary to my expectations, once I was done reading the book I decided that there was really nothing to take home from it. This, then, became a broader theme throughout my life: I have always been very weary of cults of personality and I will almost never state that I am a fan of anyone.

I say almost never, because proclaiming that nobody is worthy of admiration shows lack of appreciation for some undeniably great humans, and depending on how you mean it, it constitutes either hubris or nihilism.

So, I may, on a rare occasion, call myself a fan of someone. However, I only do so posthumously, because it is only after someone's death that we can be sure that they will not do anything stupid to disappoint us.

This is, for example, why I can say with confidence that I am a fan of Bertrand Russel, while I never said that I am a fan of Elon Musk, no matter how much I liked the guy. (And recent developments vindicate my choice amply, to say the least.)

Also, Richard Dawkins has certainly earned his laurels, but technically he is on my waiting list for as long as he is still breathing. (And in case you are wondering, no, his recent brushes with the wokes, regarding exactly how many sexes exist, which nearly resulted in him being cancelled, did not change my opinion about him at all; if anything, I have even more respect for him now.)

So, the way it went with Leonard Cohen is that I have always liked his music, but I have known very little about the man.

  • I have known him as Canadian, but that is the most basic thing you can know about someone.

  • I have known that he owns a home on the island of Hydra, where he spent a part of his life, but that is something that you cannot fail to know about him if you are Greek.

  • I have known that he is Jewish, but I have not known whether he identified as such by religion, or by heritage, or just by upbringing environment. Furthermore, I have not sought to clarify this, because I would rather leave his personal life alone.

  • I have known him as a leftist, but there are many examples of leftists who were to some degree religious.

  • I have known him as being anti-establishment, but I had no idea whether he considered god as part of the establishment.

  • I have known that he makes some religious references in his songs, but I did not have any grounds to doubt the sincerity of the references.

So, from all that I knew about him, I had no reason to suspect that he had any beef whatsoever with religion, or with god in particular.

When I discovered the song You Want it Darker on YouTube I started playing it in the background, intending to do other things while listening to it, but as soon as I realized what the lyrics were saying I jumped in my seat. I listened to it again. And again. I found the lyrics and read them. To my astonishment, I realized that the song was a fierce condemnation and rejection of the Judeo-Christian god.

The criticism in the song is not directed only towards organized religion, or only towards its followers; it is also largely directed to god himself: it is personal. And it is not just a denial: it is anathema. The song competes with old favorites of mine like Dear God by XTC, Orgasmatron by Motörhead, and God Was Never On Your Side, also by Motörhead. I cannot imagine a more poetic way of telling god to, uhm, basically, fuck off.

Acknowledging the fact that Leonard Cohen's lyrics were often enigmatic, and the fact that we tend to interpret enigmatic lyrics according to our own belief systems, I searched around for more information about the song, trying to find out what others are saying about it. Sure enough, various folks interpret the song in whatever way suits their prejudices. I found a religious web site where someone explains the song as an affirmation of Leonard Cohen's faith; so, that person listened to the same song that I listened to, and yet took home from it the exact opposite of what I took home. Great, just great.

Clearly, there must be ways of interpreting the song that are right, and ways that are wrong; but how can we tell?

Well, according to Wikipedia, Alexis Petridis, the head critic for rock and pop music at The Guardian described the song as "a menacing critique of religion".

But what do critics know, right?

And besides, everyone knows that Wikipedia is unreliable, right?

So, let us look at the lyrics, shall we?

Artist: Leonard Cohen
Song: You Want It Darker (2016)

If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game
If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame
You want it darker
We kill the flame

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the help that never came
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

There's a lover in the story
But the story's still the same
There's a lullaby for suffering
And a paradox to blame
But it's written in the scriptures
And it's not some idle claim
You want it darker
We kill the flame

They're lining up the prisoners
And the guards are taking aim
I struggle with some demons
They were middle class and tame
I didn't know I had permission
To murder and to maim
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the love that never came
You want it darker
We kill the flame

If you are the dealer, let me out of the game
If you are the healer, I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, mine must be the shame
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

For those who read the lyrics above and are still unsure, here is an explanation of it all, verse by verse, courtesy of yours truly. Of course, my interpretation may be subject to my own prejudices, so please, by all means, leave a comment and tell me where you think I am wrong.

  • If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game
    If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame
    If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame

    These verses constitute outright denial of god: whatever it is that god stands for, Leonard Cohen wants to have nothing to do with it. A reference is also being made to the biblical significance of repeating something three times as signaling a decree that is fully settled and impossible to ignore.

  • You want it darker
    We kill the flame

    These verses can be interpreted as saying that religion demands a worsening of the human condition, and its followers seem to be happy to abide to the absolute degree. The flame may allegorically refer to religion's historical opposition to enlightenment, the inescapable conclusion being that religiosity necessarily implies a dumbing down of the world. In this sense, the flame is the same as the one mentioned by another favorite Jew of mine in his own famous scathing critique of superstitious belief: The Demon-Haunted World (Science as a Candle in the Dark) by Carl Sagan. The light may also be a reference to the singer's own impending death, by way of that one poem by Dylan Thomas.

  • Magnified, sanctified
    Be thy holy name
    Vilified, crucified
    In the human frame

    "Magnified and sanctified be His great name" are the opening words of the Kaddish, a prayer central to Jewish liturgy and entirely absent from the Christian literature. The crucifixion, on the other hand, is an exclusively Christian thing, and entirely absent from the Jewish literature. Thus, these two verses establish a Judeo-Christian perspective, rather than a purely Jewish one or a purely Christian one. Obviously, Leonard Cohen has an axe to grind with both. This becomes important a bit further down.

  • A million candles burning
    For the help that never came

    This points out the folly of going through the motions of worshiping a god who is entirely absent. It also constitutes the first reference in this song of the great philosophical / theological Problem of Evil, otherwise known as the Epicurean Paradox: how is it possible to reconcile the existence of evil and suffering in this world with the notion of a supposedly omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent god? (Spoiler: it is not possible.)

  • Hineni, hineni
    I'm ready, my Lord

    Hineni is a Hebrew word which means "here I am". It is the response given by various important biblical figures, such as Abraham, upon being called by god in various chapters of the bible. In Leonard Cohen's own words, (from the official You Want It Darker press conference,) it is "a declaration of readiness, no matter what the outcome."

  • There's a lover in the story
    But the story's still the same

    The lover is obviously Jesus, since a previous verse established a Judeo-Christian context rather than a purely Jewish one. To say that the story is still the same is to say that the addition of Jesus in the New Testament does not erase the cruelty of the scriptures, nor the cruelty of the god manifested by those scriptures, and it has done nothing to lessen the historical cruelty of the followers.

  • There's a lullaby for suffering
    And a paradox to blame

    The lullaby for suffering may refer to the perverse fascination of the Christian religion with guilt to the point of self-torture. The paradox may refer either to the Epicurean Paradox, or to the famously nonsensical concept of the Original Sin.

  • But it's written in the scriptures
    And it's not some idle claim

    This is stating that all the perverse, wrongful, and inhuman things written in the scriptures cannot be simply brushed aside, and the religion has to be judged by what its own scriptures say. (If modern legal systems were to actually do that, then all Abrahamic religions would have to be outlawed as criminal organizations for incitement to hatred, racism, violence, mutilation, murder, and genocide, to name just a few of the offenses.)

  • They're lining up the prisoners
    And the guards are taking aim

    This is very obviously a reference to the holocaust.

  • I struggle with some demons
    They were middle class and tame

    The demons here are probably the conscience of all those who witnessed the holocaust and yet kept minding their own business, allowing it to happen.

  • I didn't know I had permission
    To murder and to maim

    This must be a reference to several notable accounts in the bible where god explicitly instructs the Israelites to commit genocide against their neighboring nations.

While researching the song I learned a few details about the circumstances under which it was made, which surprised me all the more. During the last year of Leonard Cohen's life, his deteriorating health severely restricted his mobility; so, the living room of his home was turned into a recording studio to allow him to sing while seated or reclining.

This means that the record was created while Leonard Cohen was fully aware that his end was near.

There is not a shadow of a doubt that when he says "I am ready, my Lord" he is acknowledging his own imminent death.

Now, usually, people on their deathbed do not tend to pick that as the best moment to break ties with god. Or should I say, to burn their bridges with god. Or perhaps, in his particular case, should I say, to napalm-bomb their bridges with god.

So, the making of this song by Leonard Cohen at the very end of his life seems to be the exact antithesis of a death-bed conversion.

Perhaps good old Leonard associated with religion during his life purely out of social interest, (like my own father did,) which may have given people some false impressions, so perhaps he wanted to set the record straight before departing.

He surely did.

In no uncertain terms.

I take my hat off to him.

The man: Leonard Cohen (Wikipedia)
The record: You Want it Darker (Wikipedia)
The song: Yow Want it Darker (Song) (Wikipedia)

item.title: On the Tired Light Hypothesis
item.description:
The Static Universe

The first model of cosmology that I was exposed to, as a small child, was that of the static universe, because that's all my father knew. According to that model, the universe is infinite in all directions, it is eternal, and it is not going anywhere. Of course I accepted it, because that is what kids do: accept everything presented to them as fact.

The Expanding Universe

Then, during elementary school, I heard of the Big Bang and the expansion of the universe; this new model of cosmology made me feel a bit uncomfortable, but again I accepted it, because a) that's what the scientists said, and b) I could go to my father and tell him that he is wrong.

The Cosmological Red-Shift

Later, during my junior high-school years, I heard of the red-shift of galaxies, as simply the Doppler effect applied to light, and it sounded reasonable, but then I heard of cosmological red-shift, as the stretching of photon wavelengths due to expansion of space itself. That sounded very exotic to me. I was again willing to accept it, because scientists had said so, but I was now starting to feel uncomfortable, because I am not into pretending to understand things that I do not truly understand. (Furthermore, my father had no concept of such things, so I could not even start a discussion with him with the goal of showing him that he is wrong.)

The Accelerating Expansion

Then I started hearing of truly bizarre observations, such as that galaxies in all directions around us are red-shifted, meaning that they are all moving away from us. When I want to comically express my bewilderment at this, I raise my arms, smell my armpits, and say "why, what's wrong with us?"

I learned that according to red-shift observations, the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us, and that not only the galaxies are moving away from each other, but the rate at which they are moving is increasing, meaning that galaxies are accelerating away from each other. Again I accepted all that because scientists had said so, but by that time it was already clear to me that I was accepting these things only because I had no other option. A little something in me was finding all this uncomfortable to the point of being disturbing.

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The apex of my discomfort came during my last year of senior high-school, when I started hearing of dark matter and dark energy; popular media portrayed them as discoveries, but a closer examination of what the scientists were actually saying revealed that they were nothing but fictitious notions that scientists had dreamt up in order to explain the observations, otherwise the numbers did not add up. In other words, the scientists had given names to their ignorance. And it was not just some small discrepancies that these novelties were called to correct for; dark matter and dark energy were supposed to account for about 95% of the universe. On the surface I was okay with this, because again, scientists had said so, but that little something in me had now started finding all this quite preposterous and becoming genuinely disturbed.

Stop for a moment and think how arrogant this is on our behalf: we are saying "here are our observations of the universe," and "here are our theories to explain those observations," and "by the way, our theories only explain 5% of the observations, the remaining 95% is inexplicable." And instead of admitting that our theories are worthless, we take it for granted that they are correct, and we assume that there must be some other, as of yet completely unknown, and completely unobserved mechanisms at play, which account for the missing 95%, so that our theories end up being correct. To top it all off, we come up with a couple of cool names for those mechanisms, to make the public think that we actually have a clue as to what we are talking about.

And wait, that's not all; we are even saying that other than exerting gravitational pull, dark matter does not seem to interact with regular matter, not even with itself, so it is virtually unobservable. This inevitably brings to mind the skeptic argument about the invisible, untouchable, and odorless realm of the supernatural as being virtually indistinguishable from the non-existent. To put it in more scientific terms, is this shit even falsifiable?

My Idea

All this was so disturbing to me, that in order to retain my sanity I was forced to invest some thinking into it, despite the hopelessness of the endeavor, given that I have no formal background in physics, let alone astrophysics; my field is, and has always been, software engineering.

My thinking was, necessarily, simple:

There is no doubt that relative movement of galaxies in space is at least partially responsible for the observed red-shift, just as it is responsible for the few cases of observed blue-shift. For example the Andromeda galaxy is blue-shifted, because it is on a collision course with the Milky Way. However, this does not mean that relative movement is necessarily responsible for all of the observed red-shift. Can we find some additional means of explaining red-shift so that we might account for those manifestations of it that are truly bizarre?

I tried to think what it means to say that the fabric of space is expanding. How do we know that it is expanding? Could it be that the only way that we know that it is expanding is due to the observed red-shift? If so, then what is the difference, really, between saying that the fabric of space is expanding, and saying that the frequency of light that is dropping? How do we know that it is one and not the other?

Thus, I arrived at my hypothesis: If light happens to have an as of yet unknown property which causes its frequency to ever so slightly decrease as it travels through the vast expanses of intergalactic space, then clearly, the result would appear as red-shift. That would beautifully explain at least two observations that are currently receiving disturbing explanations:

  • Light reaching us from any galaxy has to travel a long distance, therefore all galaxies should appear red-shifted, as they indeed do, even though they might be more or less stationary with respect to us. This is a much simpler explanation than to say that all galaxies are running away from us as if we have smelly armpits.
  • Light reaching us from distant galaxies has to travel a longer distance than from nearby galaxies, therefore more distant galaxies should appear more red-shifted, as they indeed do. This is a much simpler explanation than to say that galaxies are not only moving away from us, but actually accelerating away from us.

I knew that my idea had at least a tiny bit of merit due to Occam's razor: sure, I was postulating the existence of some hypothetical property of light that causes its frequency to decrease as it travels through space, but:

  1. This is not a terribly implausible thing to suppose, and

  2. It seems far less implausible than proposing an expanding universe, an expanding fabric of space, plus dark matter and dark energy to make the numbers add up.

Simply put, Occam's razor says that if two hypotheses have equal explaining power, the simpler one wins. What remained to be seen was whether my hypothesis did actually have equal explaining power as the established scientific theories. I suspected it did not, due to reasons beyond my level of comprehension of the universe, but I had no one to ask, and therefore no way of knowing.

I had this idea in my late teens, and not knowing what to do with it, I stored it in the back of my mind and went on with my life.

Asking around

When I was at California State University, San Bernardino I had a cool professor who came to the classroom one day with an inflatable balloon that had galaxies printed on it. By inflating the balloon, she showed how the expansion of the fabric of space can explain the observation that all galaxies are seemingly moving away from us, as well as from each other; I could accept this, but it only took care of the smelly armpits problem; the highly exotic notion of an expanding fabric of space was still there, the troublesome acceleration of the expansion was also still there, and the preposterous notions of dark matter and dark energy were still there. So, I felt that my hypothesis had lost virtually none of its explanatory merit.

During the mid 2000s, in the golden era of internet blogs, and before facebook destroyed everything, I happened to have access to an audience of a few thousand people with higher than average education. A sizable portion of them were necessarily scientists, so a few of them were bound to be astrophysicists. This prompted me to describe my idea on my blog and ask if anyone had heard of anything similar to it. Sure enough, a couple of folks stepped up to inform me that my idea had already been considered by scientists, and that although not completely devoid of scientific merit, it was regarded as false, and it had pretty much been proven wrong by experimental observations. It even had a name: The Tired Light Hypothesis.

That was an elating moment for me; there I was, a lay-person with respect to astrophysics, who had, entirely independently, and at a relatively young age, arrived at a hypothesis that had also been considered by actual astrophysicists. I figured that was a substantial accomplishment, even if the hypothesis did not turn out to be correct.

Of course it would have been even more elating if they had said "hey, wow, we never thought of this, and you know what? you might actually be right!" but let us be serious, what are the chances of that happening?

Fringe Theories

I am weary of the phenomenon of fringe theories, where certain ideas seem to exert an irresistible appeal to non-scientists, causing misinformation to spread. I also happen to be somewhat partial to another fringe theory, which is the Aquatic Ape Hypothesis, and while delving into it back in the early '90s I witnessed the controversy that it stirred: large numbers of non-biologists loving it, virtually every biologist wishing that it would just die so that people would stop pestering them with it. When David Attenborough endorsed the hypothesis, the scientific community very nearly cancelled him. Even I, despite the fact that I liked the hypothesis, thought that it had been kind of risky on his behalf to endorse it. So, I am fully aware of the fact that these are fringe theories, and I am not insisting on anything, I am just amused at how much explanatory power they have. I regard them as very interesting curiosities.

In conclusion I cannot help but mention that it gives me a warm, fuzzy feeling to keep note, somewhere in the back of my mind, of the fact that Continental Drift was also, for a long time, regarded by the scientific community as nothing but a fringe theory.

See Wikipedia: Static Universe
See Wikipedia: Big Bang
See Wikipedia: Expansion of the universe
See Wikipedia: Tired Light
See Wikipedia: Fringe Theory

item.title: The Nostradamus hoax
item.description:
The following quatrain has been circulating on the Net, attributed to Nostradamus:

In the City of Gold there will be a great thunder, Two brothers torn apart by Chaos, while the fortress endures, the great leader will succumb. The third big war will begin when the big city is burning.

This page says that the quatrain is bogus.

Also try searching here to see for yourself that no such quatrain exists among Nostradamus' writings.
